governor_removals.read: The 'law the bank objected to in writing' shape was tested for Germany and is closed: the Bundesbank's own Pressenotizen of 23 March 2001 (Stellungnahme des Zentralbankrats zur Reform der Bundesbankstruktur und der Finanzmarktaufsicht) and 22 March 2002 were both read in full, and in both the bank supports the federal finance ministry's restructuring of the Bundesbank Act rather than objecting to it. The 2002 statutory rewrite is filed above as a law change with that support stated plainly in the record, so a reader is not left thinking the bank resisted. I considered and rejected the September 2010 departure of Executive Board member Thilo Sarrazin: the application for his dismissal came from the Bundesbank's own board, so it is the bank acting on itself rather than a state organ acting on the bank, even though the Federal President is the dismissing organ.

REFUSED at round 70, and the reasoning settles a question this row had not faced squarely. The record offered was the Act amending the Bundesbank Act passed by the Bundesrat on 22 March 2002, which replaced the old governing structure with an eight-member Executive Board and ended the statutory reserved competences of the Direktorium and the Land central banks. That is a real restructuring of a central bank by the federal government -- and THE BANK SUPPORTED IT. The agent that found it also found the Zentralbankrat's Stellungnahme of 23 March 2001 backing the ministry's restructuring and the Bundesbank's own Pressenotiz of 22 March 2002 welcoming the change, and flagged the problem itself rather than filing quietly. THE RULE: this row records the state moving AGAINST the bank, and where the bank's own governing council consented in writing there is no adversary and nothing was done to it against its will. That is the converse of the caveat already written into the Nicaragua record, which says to reverse it if a round ever decides that a bank which GAINS power has not been moved against. A bank that consented has not been moved against either. Germany already holds a record on this row -- the 1997 plan to change the Bundesbank law and revalue its gold, which the bank's council called a possible attack on its independence -- so nothing is lost by refusing this one, and the contrast between the two is exactly the point: in 1997 the bank objected and in 2002 it agreed. The separate objection route was also closed this round: there is no German instance found of a law the Bundesbank opposed in writing beyond the 1997 episode already filed, and the September 2010 Sarrazin departure was considered and rejected because the dismissal application came from the Bundesbank's own board rather than from an organ of the state.
